title: Friedberg splitting

based_on.title: Lecture notes in Computability Theory
based_on.pages: December 3, 2008 version; section 30, Theorem 30.1, pp.61–62; section 31, Proposition 31.2, pp.66–67; idle-aware fresh arrivals and guarded oracle program expanded

summary: Partition any noncomputable enumerable set into two noncomputable enumerable pieces, then recover each piece using the union as an oracle.
abstract: A program can enumerate the positive answers to an undecidable membership problem. Can those answers be distributed between two enumerations while keeping both resulting problems undecidable? Friedberg splitting says this can be done for every noncomputable enumerable input set. We assign each fresh input member to one side, giving priority to requirements that oppose a proposed enumerable complement. If either side became computable, its alleged complement would unexpectedly give an ordinary decision procedure for the original input. The resulting pieces remain linked: an oracle for their union can decide each one by first checking membership in the union and only then searching their enumerations. Together the two pieces therefore carry exactly the information in the original set.
